title: Simplify editor game speed implementation
body:
### This PR is the de facto industry standard for time scaling.
It is used in e.g. UNITY, UNREAL, CRYENGINE / O3DE, DEFOLD, SOURCE.
_No other major engine uses tick fudging for time scaling (the method this PR reverts)._

The PR contains three commits:
* reverts the backend implementation (but not the UI) of #107273
* adds adjustment to game speed by a simple wall clock multiplier via `OS::set_primary_time_scale()`, and calls it from the editor speed UI
* calls the _raw_ (unscaled) version in select locations for profiling, network

`OS::get_ticks_usec() / msec` now returns scaled (fluid) time
`OS::get_ticks_usec_raw() / msec` now returns the raw time from the OS

This is _currently_ compiled out in release and passes through so that there is no scaling in release (_it can easily be made to work in release if desired, for example if we want users to be able to use "bullet time" effects in games._).

Fixes #122242.
Fixes #122217.

Simpler (non-UI) implementation for https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12555.
This is a production version of #123462 (which was a proof of concept, simpler conceptually to test the waters).

## Explanation
It is possible to modify game speed with no other modifications to the engine simply by changing how the wall clock progresses.

I wasn't party to the original proposal / implementation. It seems overly complicated and bug-prone, for something that can likely be kept very simple. The current implementation also seems to be passing complexity on to users, hence the above issues. The approach taken this PR of scaling the wall clock is imo a far more sensible approach to take longterm for editor game speed modification than attempting to fudge physics tick rates (the current approach), which will break a number of underlying engine systems.

### `OS::get_ticks_usec_raw()`
Although most engine systems work fine simply modifying the wall clock, there are a small number of engine systems that benefit from accessing the raw (non-scaled) wall clock. This PR provides this ability through the renamed `OS::get_ticks_usec_raw()` and `OS::get_ticks_msec_raw()`  function.

Examples include audio, network, profiling and some performance throttling. This is included in the third commit. (The third commit is not attempting to be exhaustive, but should cover the major cases.) Profiling and performance throttling are non-critical, but audio can glitch if starved of tile refreshes, and networking often benefits from real time for synchronization and timeouts etc.

#### Alternative
_An obvious alternative is to have `get_ticks_usec()` return raw ticks, and another function like `get_scaled_ticks_usec()` only for the time scaled version. It depends which would cause the greater churn. In this case, it seems only a few places benefit from access to the raw version, and doing it this way keeps it compatible for third party code._

## Final production version
As such this contains some additions since #123462:

* backward compatibility - stubs for APIs introduced by #107273 which are now redundant
* lockless - the main `get_ticks_usec()` is lockless using atomics and the sequence lock pattern
* calls the _raw_ version to make realtime systems more consistent even when changing wall clock scale

## Comparison of the existing approach (change ticks per second) versus this PR (change wall clock)

### Existing approach
* wall clock and tick numbers will diverge wildly
* anything calculating logic via time-keeping singletons (`OS` / `Time` ticks) will outpace the game state
* gameplay timers / cool-down cycles tracking real time will completely detach from character movements / physical animations
* breaks physics interpolation
* integer tick rates cause rounding errors, this causes glitches, quantized physics delta (like 1/48 instead of 1/60) enter simulation and user code. This changes actual speed and behaviour of gravity, friction and velocities inside `_physics_process`.

### This PR
* everything *just works* :tm: game logic, animations, interpolation all change speed
* potential regressions are isolated to a small number of areas requiring real time : especially audio and network
* the above are almost all likely to be _outside_ user code, so changes to the speed are transparent to user projects

## Compatibility
#### Derived OSes should rename their function to `get_ticks_usec_raw()`
As the objective is to change the functionality of `get_ticks_usec()` to be a wrapper, afaik we either have to introduce a new wrapper function (e.g. `get_ticks_usec_scaled()`) _or_ we have to rename the function that is wrapped (the raw timing).

Rather than change all calling sites (which is a lot of places, and present in third party code), the easiest way to do this is to rename the raw timing function that will be in the derived OSes.

This does mean that anyone with a fork of the engine that has used their own OS will need to rename their `get_ticks_usec()` function to `get_ticks_usec_raw()`. This is a tiny breakage that should only occur for a few cases, and it's easily solvable by a rename (or a rename with a macro switch based on the engine version, whichever is preferred). So I can't see this being a problem in practice, for the significant stability gains we are getting here.

#### Third party code that absolutely requires realtime timings should call `get_ticks_usec_raw()`
Additionally, any third party code that *needs* access to raw timings should switch over to using the `get_ticks_usec_raw()` API. However that should be rare, as in most cases the objective of editor game scaling _is_ to scale the timings reported.

## Multiplayer
Multiplayer is very unlikely to work with timescaling _at all_ (either using this version or the old). As such I haven't converted any of the multiplayer networking to use `raw` functions, to prevent git noise. Having different clients in a multiplayer work at different timescales doesn't really even make sense in the conventional sense way anyway, because networking relies on synchronised timing.

## Notes
* As ever, I'm happy to rename functions / shift things around as desired by reviewers
* The _raw_ function is not currently bound. This is deliberate, and should only be bound imo if it proves it _needs_ to be used (i.e. there is a provable use case).
* The interesting part here is the second commit, which is the implementation for the new system.
* Fills a sync point everytime the wall clock scale is changed.
* Each call to `get_ticks_usec()` is measured relative to the previous sync point.
* Accuracy is kept high, but 128 bit fixed point is used to prevent overflow.
* Using floating point isn't recommended over a large timer range where accuracy can become a problem. Fixed point bypasses this ensuring stable behaviour over the entire `uint64_t` range.
* It is still theoretically possible to overflow the `uint64_t` when using a timer and a very high game speed. Recovering from this is not straightforward, so it's not dealt with .. it's unlikely to happen in the wild. At scale 1.0, Godot can run for 585 thousand years without overflow. So even at 500x gamespeed, Godot could still run for over a thousand years, which seems enough. :thinking:
* Although profiling is a little more accurate using the raw timings when the game is scaled, these profilings are never going to be that useful anyway (there's even an argument to not bother, and just use the scaled timings in all profiling cases).
* Research showed that all the major game engines also follow this approach, they also expose both the scaled timing functions and an unscaled version ("raw" in this PR).

## Addendum - "bullet time"
This also (coincidentally) is exactly a recommended way of implementing "bullet time" like "the matrix".
If desired we can add this feature, it might require:
* compiling in wall clock scaling in release
* adding a timescaling "fade" helper (to get smooth fades in time scaling, rather than abrupt changes)
* adding a scene tree mechanism to allow excluding nodes from bullet time (e.g. UI etc).

The mechanism is different that the existing game timescaling (available in 3.x) which isn't particularly useful afaik, maybe that could be shoehorned to use this method, but that might be breaking compatibility.
